Management strategies for stable angina should be tailored to the individual patient, rather than follow a structured hierarchical regimen. Microvascular dysfunction is gaining recognition as an important driver of symptoms, yet pharmacologic development has not kept pace with this need. Advances in invasive diagnostics and novel interventions, including regenerative approaches, represent promising avenues for future care.

Introduction Chronic stable angina remains a common and challenging clinical problem, reflecting both obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD) and increasingly recognized conditions such as coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD) and vasospastic angina. Despite advances in revascularization and preventive therapy, many patients continue to experience angina, contributing to impaired quality of life, recurrent hospitalizations, and increased healthcare utilization. This review aims to provide an updated synthesis of contemporary pharmacologic and interventional options for angina, with particular attention to adjunctive and emerging therapies.

Search Methodology and Scope of Review This is a narrative review. To capture the breadth of contemporary evidence, we conducted a focused literature search of the PubMed library, using combinations of keywords including angina, antianginal therapy, coronary microvascular dysfunction, vasospastic angina, and optimal medical therapy. Peer-reviewed clinical trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and major guideline statements were considered for inclusion. Case reports, non-peer-reviewed articles, and publications not available in English were excluded. The review prioritizes evidence from randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses when available, while incorporating observational studies and expert consensus where data are limited.

Aims and Objectives The aim of this review is to provide a comprehensive overview of contemporary antianginal therapy. Specifically, we summarize the evidence supporting established first-line and adjunctive pharmacotherapies, highlight the role of emerging agents and interventional approaches with particular attention to coronary microvascular dysfunction and vasospastic angina, and place these therapeutic strategies within the context of current guideline recommendations. Throughout, we emphasize the importance of patient-centered and individualized care in the management of stable angina.

Optimal Medical Therapy and Antianginals Optimal medical therapy (OMT) for stable angina aims to reduce the lifetime risk of cardiovascular events while alleviating angina symptoms. Optimizing cardiovascular risk factors remains a cornerstone of comprehensive care: strict blood pressure control in patients with hypertension, lipid management with high-intensity statins (and adjunctive therapy as indicated), glycemic optimization in diabetes, smoking cessation to reduce vasospastic triggers, and weight management to improve exercise tolerance. Additional considerations include treatment of anemia, evaluation and management of obstructive sleep apnea, adherence to a heart-healthy diet, and psychosocial support for comorbid depression or anxiety. Such holistic care improves long-term cardiovascular outcomes and may also directly reduce anginal burden in selected patients. While the broader management of coronary artery disease encompasses these preventive strategies, this review will focus specifically on antianginal therapies.

OMT has historically been framed by a tiered approach, beginning with beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers (CCBs), and nitrates as first-line agents before advancing to other second-line agents. This traditional model is largely rooted in expert opinion rather than strong comparative evidence [ 1 , 2 ]. Recent definitions of OMT emphasize symptom control and the prevention of cardiac events associated with stable CAD, with maximal patient adherence and minimal adverse events [ 1 , 3 ].

However, OMT is often underutilized in clinical practice. A large registry analysis showed that less than half of patients with stable CAD undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) were on appropriate doses of antianginal therapy prior to the procedure [ 4 ]. Similarly, the Angina Prevalence and Provider Evaluation of Angina Relief (APPEAR) study illustrated wide variability in real-world prescribing patterns, with just over half of patients with frequent angina prescribed two or more antianginal medications [ 5 ]. The Objective Randomized Blinded Investigation with Optimal Medical Therapy of Angioplasty in Stable Angina (ORBITA) trial further added perspective by showing that a structured 6-week protocolized medical optimization phase prior to PCI improved symptoms significantly, and that PCI did not provide additional benefit over OMT alone in improving exercise time, symptom severity, or quality of life in patients with stable angina [ 6 ].

Akin to the management of hypertension, angina management should take advantage of a broad therapeutic toolbox, with treatment decisions guided by comorbidities, hemodynamics, and medication tolerance [ 1 ]. In addition, an optimal treatment plan should emphasize patient preferences. A study of patients with comparable angina severity and functional limitations found wide variation in willingness to accept risk for symptom relief, with some patients more willing to accept increased mortality risk or forgo years of life to be free of angina [ 7 ]. This highlights the importance for shared decision-making and patient-centered goals in defining OMT.

First-Line Antianginal Therapies For most patients with stable angina, initial therapy typically begins with either beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers. Both the 2024 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and the 2023 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC) guidelines recommend either of these agents as first-line therapy in patients without contraindications, with subsequent addition of other antianginal drugs when symptom control is inadequate. The ESC guidelines place greater emphasis on individualizing therapy, noting that no antianginal class demonstrated clear superiority over another for symptom relief [ 8 , 9 ].

Head-to-head trials and meta-analyses, beginning with the landmark study by Heidenreich et al., have consistently shown no significant differences in anginal relief or major clinical outcomes between beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, and nitrates in regards to anginal relief [ 10 ]. More recent systematic reviews that included newer agents, such as ranolazine and ivabradine, have reached similar conclusions. However, the available evidence is limited by a paucity of newer randomized trials directly comparing agents, highlighting the need for individualized therapy guided by comorbidities, hemodynamic, and patient tolerance rather than rigid drug class hierarchies [ 11 ].

Beta-Blockers Overview and Mechanism of Action Beta-blockers remain a cornerstone of angina management. By lowering heart rate, blood pressure, and myocardial contractility, they reduce myocardial oxygen demand and improve coronary perfusion [ 12 , 13 ]. In additino, beta-blockers inhibit renin release [ 12 , 14 ].

Indications Beta-blockers are indicated for the management of stable angina, particularly in patients with a history of prior myocardial infarction (MI), left ventricular (LV) dysfunction, or obstructive CAD. They are a key component of therapy for patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and may provide benefit in individuals with microvascular dysfunction by reducing ischemic burden through improved myocardial oxygen supply–demand balance. Additional indications include concomitant hypertension and rate control in patients with atrial fibrillation or a history of other supraventricular tachyarrhythmias.

In the context of chronic coronary disease or stable ischemic heart disease, the indication for beta-blockers depends on underlying myocardial function and comorbidities. Currently, the strongest evidence for long-term beta-blocker use is in patients with prior MI and reduced ejection fraction (EF).

For patients with concomitant hypertension, third-generation beta-blockers such as carvedilol and nebivolol may offer added benefits. Carvedilol is a nonselective beta-blocker with alpha-1 blocking and antioxidant properties that reduce peripheral vascular resistance and may improve insulin sensitivity compared with traditional beta-blockers. Nebivolol, a highly selective beta-1 blocker, promotes nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation and enhances endothelial function [ 15 ].

Clinical Evidence While often chosen as the first-line agent, the preference for beta-blockers over other antianginal medications is not fully supported by evidence [ 10 , 16 ]. An early meta-analysis by Heidenreich and colleagues compared beta-blockers, CCB, and nitrates among patients with stable angina, finding similar clinical outcomes amongst the medication classes. Rates of cardiac death and MI were similar across medication classes. However, patients treated with beta-blockers exhibited slightly improved anginal relief with fewer adverse effects and lower rates of discontinuation (0.31 less angina episodes per week compared with CCBs and 0.63 less episodes compared with nitrates) [ 10 ]. A more recent meta-analysis suggests that while beta-blockers may improve mortality and reduce rates of unstable angina compared with no treatment, they do not provide superior antianginal relief compared with other medication classes [ 16 ].

The Total Ischaemic Burden European Trial (TIBET) compared atenolol, nifedipine, and their combination through standardized exercise testing and 48-h ambulatory ST-segment monitoring. The study found no significant differences among the groups in the reduction of ischemic episodes. However, combination therapy resulted in a greater reduction in blood pressure than either agent alone [ 17 ]. Beta-blockers can be used in combination with dihydropyridines to counteract dihydropyridine-induced tachycardia, although the additional benefit of this approach is unclear [ 17 – 19 ]. The addition of nifedipine to beta-blockers may offer greater anginal relief compared with the addition of long-acting nitrates to beta-blockers [ 20 ].

The mortality and morbidity benefits of beta-blockers in patients with LV systolic dysfunction, irrespective of prior MI, are well established. However, in the contemporary era of routine revascularization, high statin use, and dual antiplatelet therapy, the long-term prognostic benefit of beta-blockers in patients with preserved LV function after MI has been questioned. Current evidence suggests the addition of a beta-blocker in this population does not reduce the composite endpoint of all-cause mortality or new MI compared with no beta-blocker use [ 21 , 22 ]. Several ongoing trials aim to further clarify their role in patients with stable ischemic heart disease and preserved ejection fraction [ 23 – 25 ]. In this context, beta-blockers should be prescribed primarily for symptom control, with dosing titrated to alleviate angina rather than to achieve maximally tolerated doses.

Dosing and Titration When considering the use of beta-blockers in the management of angina, several important factors must be carefully evaluated to ensure optimal patient outcomes and minimize potential risks. AHA/ACC guidelines suggest that beta-blocker doses be titrated to maintain a resting heart rate between 55 and 60 beats per minute (bpm), or even 50 bpm in patients with recalcitrant angina [ 8 ]. Nevertheless, many patients on beta blockade maintain a heart rate > 70 bpm, with accompanying worsened health outcomes and increased angina burden [ 26 ]. A study conducted in China by Jiang et al. demonstrated that a higher daily dose of metoprolol succinate (190 mg) was more effective in achieving the target heart rate compared with a lower daily dose of 95 mg. The study did not specify whether the dosing regimen involved multiple administrations or a single daily dose [ 27 ].

In patients with HFrEF, beta-blockers should be titrated to the maximally tolerated dose. However, no optimal dosing has been established for patients with stable angina without heart failure (HF). Amongst the studies analyzed by Heidenreich et al., mean daily doses included atenolol 95 mg, metoprolol 177 mg, bisoprolol 10 mg, and carvedilol 50 mg. In patients without HF, titration of beta-blockers or the addition of another agent is recommended to achieve heart rate targets and symptomatic relief. There are few trials comparing the efficacy of different beta-blockers. Earlier studies from the noncontemporary era reported no significant differences in angina reduction between specific beta-blockers, such as propranolol, oxprenolol, practolol, metoprolol, and tolamolol [ 28 , 29 ].

Contraindications and Tolerability Beta-blockers are absolutely contraindicated in cases of severe bradycardia and advanced heart block and remain relatively contraindicated in patients with reactive airway disease, severe depression, vasospastic angina, or diabetes characterized by frequent hypoglycemic episodes. One retrospective UK primary care cohort study revealed significant discontinuation rates of beta-blockers in patients with stable angina, with 55% discontinuing therapy within 3 years compared with 43% in patients having experienced MI [ 30 ]. When adverse events occurred, patients with angina were nearly twice as likely to discontinue therapy completely (11.3% versus 5.9% in patients having experienced MI). Furthermore, 71.5% of patients with angina received no dose titration after initial prescription, potentially contributing to suboptimal treatment outcomes [ 30 ]. This emphasizes the importance of reassessing patients’ anginal symptoms and medication requirements following beta-blocker initiation. A meta-analysis found that beta-blockers were discontinued owing to adverse events less often than calcium channel blockers, with an odds ratio of 0.72 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.60–0.86) [ 10 ].

Calcium Channel Blockers Overview and Mechanism of Action Calcium channel blockers are a widely used class of antianginal medications that improve myocardial oxygen balance through vasodilation and, in some cases, reduction in heart rate and contractility. Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (non-DHPs) reduce myocardial oxygen demand through negative chronotropic and inotropic effects, while also promoting coronary vasodilation, increasing myocardial oxygen supply, and reducing afterload by lowering blood pressure. In contrast, dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (DHPs) (e.g., amlodipine and nifedipine) are more effective at coronary vasodilation and blood pressure reduction but lack the inotropic and chronotropic effects associated with non-DHPs [ 31 ].

Indications CCBs are indicated for the treatment of stable angina, with specific agent selection guided by comorbid conditions and hemodynamic status. DHPs are effective in patients with vasospastic angina, obstructive CAD, and hypertension, and are particularly useful in those with Raynaud phenomenon owing to their strong peripheral vasodilatory effects. Among DHPs, nifedipine has been shown to be particularly effective in reducing angina in patients with vasospastic angina [ 27 ].

Non-DHPs also play a role in the management of vasospastic angina and obstructive CAD and are especially useful in patients with coexisting atrial fibrillation or supraventricular tachycardias, where rate control is required. The use of CCBs in heart failure is more nuanced. While early studies raised concerns about worsening outcomes, these effects are drug specific [ 29 – 31 ]. For instance, nifedipine has been associated with worsening HF, whereas amlodipine is generally safe and may even offer survival benefit in patients with nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy [ 32 , 33 ]. Thus, the decision to initiate or continue CCBs in patients with HF should be made on a case-by-case basis.

Clinical Evidence Both DHPs and non-DHPs significantly reduce weekly anginal episodes and nitroglycerin use, with no clear superiority between classes [ 32 , 33 ]. A study comparing diltiazem and verapamil demonstrated greater symptomatic relief and lower resting heart rates in patients treated with diltiazem. Furthermore, the once-daily dosing regimen of diltiazem offers enhanced convenience, potentially improving adherence [ 34 ]. In contrast, when comparing nifedipine and amlodipine, neither agent demonstrates clear superiority [ 18 ].

Dosing and Titration Amlodipine offers a dose-dependent benefit in angina relief, with 10 mg daily maximizing antianginal efficacy [ 35 ]. Similarly, the extended-release formulation of nifedipine at 60–90 mg daily demonstrates greater efficacy in treating angina compared with lower doses [ 20 , 36 ]. Dosing should be titrated according to symptom control, blood pressure, and adverse effects.

Contraindications and Tolerability Common side effects of CCBs include flushing, headache, dizziness, and peripheral edema, the latter being more common with dihydropyridines such as amlodipine and nifedipine [ 37 , 38 ]. Non-dihydropyridines are contraindicated in patients with bradycardia or atrioventricular block owing to their negative chronotropic effects. Compared with non-DHPs, DHPs are generally better tolerated, as they do not suppress heart rate or contractility. However, verapamil in particular is associated with gastrointestinal side effects, such as constipation. Agent selection should be tailored to the individual patient’s comorbidities, hemodynamic profile, and risk of adverse effects.

Adjunctive Antianginal Agents Nitrates Overview and Mechanism of Action Nitrates are vasodilators that exert their anti-ischemic effects by being metabolized into nitric oxide (NO), which activates the cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) pathway, leading to vascular smooth muscle relaxation. Peripheral venous dilation results in reduced preload, thereby reducing myocardial wall tension and oxygen demand. Nitrates also dilate epicardial arteries, lower blood pressure, and may inhibit platelet aggregation, all further contributing to their anti-ischemic properties [ 39 , 40 ].

Indications Nitrates are indicated for the acute relief and prophylaxis of angina. Short-acting nitrates (e.g., sublingual nitroglycerin tablets or spray) are used for the immediate treatment of acute anginal episodes or as prophylaxis before physical exertion. Long-acting nitrates (e.g., isosorbide mononitrate, isosorbide dinitrate and nitroglycerin patches) are typically used as adjunct therapy in patients who remain symptomatic despite treatment with beta-blockers or CCBs.

Clinical Evidence A study comparing nitroglycerin spray to tablet formulations found that spray was superior in providing faster pain relief and reduced the number of anginal attacks, with fewer associated headaches, compared with tablet [ 41 ]. Despite the clinical advantages of the spray formulation, the tablet formulation is more commonly utilized owing to ease of use and cost [ 42 , 43 ]. The spray formulation requires additional steps, such as device priming, and is often more expensive and less available. Furthermore, some patients report taste disturbances with the spray formulation, which may influence preference [ 41 ].

Data comparing long-acting nitrates with beta-blockers or calcium antagonists are limited. Available evidence suggests that long-acting nitrates may be less effective compared with beta-blockers and CCBs in reducing anginal episodes, with some studies showing a non-statistically significant trend toward more frequent angina in patients using long-acting nitrates [ 10 ].

Dosing and Titration Short-acting nitrates are administered sublingually or as a spray at the onset of angina or prior to activities known to precipitate symptoms. Among long-acting nitrates, isosorbide mononitrate, compared with isosorbide dinitrate, has a higher bioavailability (100%) and a longer half-life, allowing for once-daily dosing [ 44 ]. Previous studies comparing once-daily nitrate dosing versus multiple-dose found better quality-of-life indices with once-daily dosing and better patient compliance with isosorbide mononitrate [ 45 , 46 ]. In contrast, isosorbide dinitrate undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism, resulting in variable bioavailability and a shorter half-life.

Contraindications and Tolerability The most common side effect of nitrates is headache, secondary to vasodilation. Other potential side effects include dizziness, flushing, syncope, and orthostatic hypotension. Nitrates are contraindicated in patients taking phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) inhibitors owing to the risk of severe hypotension, as well as in those with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or severe aortic stenosis, limiting the patient populations this drug class can be used in.

Ranolazine Overview and Mechanism of Action Ranolazine is an antianginal agent thought to inhibit the late inward sodium current in ischemic myocytes, which reduces calcium overload by promoting calcium outflow through the Na⁺–Ca 2+ exchanger, thereby lowering LV diastolic tension. This reduction in LV tension is thought to enhance coronary blood flow [ 47 ].

Indications Ranolazine is approved for the treatment of chronic stable angina, particularly as an adjunctive agent in patients who remain symptomatic despite other therapies. It is especially useful in patients with low resting heart rate or low blood pressure, where the use of other antianginal agents may be limited owing to hemodynamic effects. Because ranolazine has a minimal impact on heart rate and blood pressure, it provides a unique therapeutic option in this setting. Ranolazine may also offer benefit in patients with microvascular dysfunction, although more evidence is needed to define its role in this population.

Clinical Evidence The Metabolic Efficiency With Ranolazine for Less Ischemia in Non-ST-Elevation Acute Coronary Syndromes (MERLIN)-TIMI 36 trial showed that adding ranolazine to standard therapy for non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome (ACS) did not reduce cardiovascular death, MI, or recurrent ischemia [ 48 ]. However additional analysis indicated potential benefits in reducing recurrent ischemic episodes and the need for additional antianginal medications in patients with established ischemic heart disease [ 48 ]. The Efficacy of Ranolazine in Chronic Angina (ERICA) trial further supported its role as adjunctive therapy, showing reduced angina frequency and nitroglycerin use in patients with persistent symptoms despite maximal amlodipine doses [ 49 ]. Other trials, including the Monotherapy Assessment of Ranolazine In Stable Angina (MARISA) and the Combination Assessment of Ranolazine In Stable Angina (CARISA) trials, have shown improvements in exercise tolerance and symptom onset in patients with chronic angina taking ranolazine [ 50 – 52 ].

In addition to its antianginal effects, post hoc analysis of the MERLIN-TIMI 36 trial found that patients treated with ranolazine had lower glycated hemoglobin (HbA1C) compared with placebo, suggesting benefit in patients with diabetes [ 53 ]. Further studies have confirmed the utility of ranolazine as an adjunct to antidiabetic therapy in patients with cardiovascular disease and poorly controlled diabetes. A meta-analysis of ranolazine in patients with diabetes found a weighted mean decrease in A1c of 0.49% compared with placebo [ 54 ]. The recent Characterising Mechanisms in Patients with Coronary Microvascular Disease to Stratify Therapy (ChaMP-CMD) trial contributed to existing evidence and demonstrated that patients with objective evidence of impaired coronary flow reserve (CFR) had significant improvements in treadmill exercise time when treated with ranolazine or amlodipine and in Seattle Angina Questionnaire (SAQ) summary score with ranolazine but not amlodipine [ 55 ]. While the mechanism of ranolazine’s glucose-lowering properties is not fully understood, animal models suggest blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels in pancreatic alpha cells, leading to reduced glucagon secretion [ 56 ].

Dosing and Titration Ranolazine is typically initiated at 500 mg twice daily, with uptitration to 1000 mg twice daily as tolerated [ 57 ]. It has minimal hemodynamic effects, making it particularly useful in patients with hypotension or bradycardia.

Contraindications and Tolerability Ranolazine has a generally favorable safety profile, with a discontinuation rate of 8.8% due to adverse effects compared with 4.7% in placebo groups. Common side effects include dizziness (13% versus 7% for placebo), constipation (9% versus 3%), and nausea (9% versus 6%). While concerns exist for more serious effects such as syncope (3.3% versus 2.3%) and QT prolongation (0.9% versus 0.3%), clinical data show no significant difference in arrhythmia occurrence compared with placebo [ 48 , 50 , 51 ]. Ranolazine undergoes cytochrome-mediated metabolism and glucuronidation and is partially excreted unchanged by the kidneys, making it contraindicated in patients with renal or hepatic impairment and those taking CYP3A inhibitors or certain antiarrhythmic drugs [ 47 , 48 , 50 , 51 ].

Ivabradine Overview and Mechanism of Action Ivabradine is a selective heart rate-lowering agent that acts on the sinoatrial node by inhibiting the I(f) current, resulting in decreased heart rate and myocardial oxygen demand. However, while beta-blockers and non-DHP CCBs act on both the atrioventricular (AV) and sinoatrial (SA) nodes, ivabradine selectively inhibits the I(f) current in the sinoatrial node without affecting atrioventricular conduction [ 58 ].

Indications Ivabradine is indicated for patients with HFrEF who have a resting heart rate > 70 beats per minute despite receiving maximally tolerated guideline-directed medical therapy. In this population, it is used to further reduce heart rate and improve clinical outcomes. In patients with stable angina and HFrEF, ivabradine may be considered as an adjunct to beta-blocker therapy.

Clinical Evidence Ivabradine may improve exercise tolerance and delay symptom onset during exertion in patients with stable angina [ 58 , 59 ]. Ivabradine was found to be as effective as atenolol in reducing anginal symptoms during exercise [ 59 ]. The Practical Daily Efficacy And Safety of Procoralan in Combination with Beta-Blockers (ADDITIONS) study further demonstrated the benefits of combining ivabradine with beta-blockers, showing reduced angina frequency, improved exercise tolerance, and enhanced quality of life, as measured by the standard EuroQol 5-Dimension (EQ-5D) questionnaire [ 60 , 61 ].

Other studies have suggested that the benefit of ivabradine in reducing angina may be limited to patients with HFrEF who need additional heart rate control. The Study Assessing the Morbidity–Mortality Benefits of the If Inhibitor Ivabradine in Patients with Coronary Artery Disease (SIGNIFY) trial evaluated the effectiveness of ivabradine in patients with angina without HFrEF. The study did not find significant benefit in reducing angina or improving cardiovascular events in this patient population, even suggesting increased risk of cardiovascular events in patients with more severe angina without HFrEF [ 62 ]. Thus, in patients with activity-limiting angina without HFrEF, the use of ivabradine is not recommended. Its effectiveness in HFrEF may be due to the reliance of heart rate on cardiac output in patients with reduced systolic function, making prolonged diastolic filling time more critical. Unlike other agents, ivabradine selectively lowers heart rate without affecting contractility.

In patients with HFrEF, however, the Systolic Heart Failure Treatment with the I(f) Inhibitor Ivabradine Trial (SHIFT) reported improved clinical outcomes in patients with HFrEF taking ivabradine [ 63 ]. The SHIFT trial evaluated the addition of ivabradine to standard therapy in patients with HFrEF and heart rate > 70 bpm, finding reduced hospital admissions and improved quality-of-life measures in these patients. However, its effects on reducing cardiovascular mortality in these patients remains uncertain, with one meta-analysis suggesting no benefit [ 64 , 65 ].
Dosing and Titration Ivabradine is typically initiated at 5 mg twice daily, with uptitration to 7.5 mg twice daily as tolerated [ 66 ]. Dose reduction may be necessary if bradycardia develops.

Contraindications and Tolerability Adverse effects of ivabradine include bradycardia and phosphenes [ 58 – 60 , 67 ]. The SIGNIFY study also reported a possible risk of atrial fibrillation among ivabradine users compared with placebo, though this effect was rare [ 62 ]. Ivabradine should be avoided in patients with bradycardia, pacemaker dependence, acute decompensated HF, severe hepatic impairment, or in those taking QT interval-prolonging drugs [ 67 , 68 ]. In addition, ivabradine remains considerably more expensive in the USA compared with beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, and ranolazine, limiting accessibility.

Trimetazidine Overview and Mechanism of Action Trimetazidine offers a unique mechanism of action, shifting myocardial metabolism from fatty-acid to glucose oxidation and thus offers benefits without affecting hemodynamics. Several studies have shown that adjunctive trimetazidine therapy with traditional antianginal agents leads to improvements in angina and exercise tolerance [ 69 – 71 ].

Indications Trimetazidine is primarily used as adjunctive therapy in patients with stable angina who remain symptomatic despite optimal use of conventional agents. It may be particularly useful in patients who cannot tolerate the hemodynamic side effects of other traditional antianginals. Although used in Europe as a second-line agent for more than 40 years, it remains unapproved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in the USA, partly owing to safety concerns and lack of observed benefit in some trials, such as the Efficacy and Safety of Trimetazidine in Patients with Angina Pectoris Treated by Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (ATPCI) trial [ 67 ].

Clinical Evidence Both the Trimetazidine in Poland (TRIMPOL) I and II studies demonstrated improved anginal symptoms and exercise capacity when added to traditional therapies [ 69 , 72 ]. However, the ATPCI trial, which compared adjunctive trimetazidine therapy with placebo, alongside OMT after successful PCI, showed no improvement in long-term clinical outcomes in terms of cardiac-related hospital admissions, cardiac death, or persistence of angina [ 73 ].

Imbria Pharmaceuticals (Boston, Massachusetts) is investigating ninerafaxstat, a cardiometabolic agent with a similar mechanism of action. An ongoing phase 2 randomized, placebo-controlled study aims to evaluate the safety and efficacy of ninerafaxstat in patients with stable angina [ 74 ].

Contraindications and Tolerability While trimetazidine is generally well tolerated, it is associated with rare but typically reversible gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms or Parkinsonian symptoms, particularly in older patients or those with renal impairment and GI disturbances [ 75 ]. European regulatory agencies have recommended caution in these populations [ 76 ]. However, notably, extrapyramidal symptoms in the ATPCI trial were rare and there was no statistically significant difference between treatment and placebo groups (0.3% versus 0.2%, respectively) [ 73 ]. l -Arginine l -arginine, a precursor for NO synthesis, is anecdotally used to supplement standard medical therapy. However, evidence supporting its efficacy in patients with stable angina remains inconsistent. One study evaluated an arginine-rich medical food as an adjunct therapy in patients with class II or III angina, demonstrating improved exercise capacity, quality of life, and vascular function (as measured by flow-mediated dilation of the brachial artery using ultrasound). This supplement notably combined l -arginine with other nutrients known to enhance endothelium-derived NO [ 77 ]. In contrast, trials using l -arginine alone found no meaningful benefit, suggesting l -arginine alone may be insufficient to confer clinical benefits but may have a synergistic effect with antioxidants or other nutrients [ 78 , 79 ]. l -arginine may have a role in patients with microvascular dysfunction, where endothelial dysfunction is a key driver of symptoms. Palloshi et al. investigated the effects of l -arginine supplementation (2 g, three times a day over 4 weeks) in 13 patients with hypertension and microvascular dysfunction and noted improvements in angina class, systolic blood pressure at rest, and quality of life. In addition, objective improvements in endothelial function were observed, which were not reported in studies of patients with obstructive CAD [ 80 ]. Further research is warranted to validate its efficacy in this population.

Coronary Microvascular Dysfunction Pathophysiology and Diagnostic Challenges CMD is characterized by endothelial and smooth muscle dysfunction in the small blood vessels that supply the myocardium [ 81 ]. The myocardial microvasculature is essential for regulating blood flow in response to increasing oxygen demands, and CMD accounts for a significant portion of patients with angina with non-obstructed coronary arteries (ANOCA). It is also implicated in persistent angina following coronary revascularization [ 82 , 83 ]. In this context, tailoring antianginal medical therapy becomes especially important for optimally managing CMD.

Diagnosis of CMD can be challenging, as standard coronary angiography does not assess microvascular function. Positron emission tomography (PET) scans can provide a non-invasive method for diagnosing CMD by measuring myocardial blood flow (MBF) and CFR. The Coronary Microvascular Angina (CorMicA) trial demonstrated the value of an interventional diagnostic approach that improves outcomes by stratifying therapy on the basis of invasive physiological measurements [ 84 ]. This study assigned 151 patients without obstructive CAD into either an intervention group involving a diagnostic procedure or a control group receiving standard of care. In the angiographic intervention group, CFR, index of microcirculatory resistance (IMR), and fractional flow reserve (FFR) were measured, along with vasoreactivity testing using intracoronary acetylcholine to provoke vasospasm. This approach allowed a more comprehensive evaluation of coronary function, stratifying the patient’s angina into endotypes such as microvascular angina (MVA) versus vasospastic angina.

Both the 2024 ESC and the 2023 AHA/ACC guidelines support this framework. The ESC recommends non-invasive imaging, such as PET, cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), or stress echocardiography to measure CFR, and endorses invasive testing with CFR, IMR, and acetylcholine provocation in patients with persistent angina and non-obstructive disease [ 9 ]. The AHA/ACC guidelines are concordant, noting that invasive coronary physiology testing, including CFR, IMR, and vasoreactivity, can guide management in ischemia with non-obstructive arteries [ 8 ]. The ESC explicitly recognizes acetylcholine testing for vasospasm, though wider uptake remains limited by heterogeneity and safety concerns [ 85 ].

CMD Management A clearer diagnosis of angina etiology enables targeted medical therapy. For vasospastic angina, CCBs and nitrates are preferred, while beta-blockers may be more appropriate for CMD without vasospasm. The CorMicA study found that the interventional diagnostic procedure, combined with stratified medical therapy, significantly improved quality of life and reduced angina severity compared with standard care, with benefits attributed to individualized treatment [ 84 ]. Current guidelines for patients with MVA are similar to those with obstructive CAD [ 8 ]. Further studies directly comparing antianginal agents in patients with MVA without vasospasm are necessary to optimize treatment strategies.

The current literature for CMD treatment is limited, with most recommendations derived from small trials. Adjunctive therapies discussed previously, particularly ranolazine and ivabradine, alongside conventional antianginals such as beta-blockers, CCBs, and nitrates have been explored in this population [ 81 , 86 ]. There is insufficient evidence to suggest that either ranolazine or ivabradine is superior in this population.

A randomized trial found significant improvement in angina frequency, physical limitation, and disease perception, as well as prolonged time to 1-mm ST-segment depression and longer total exercise duration on stress testing with ranolazine [ 87 ]. However, a 2016 placebo-controlled trial found no significant improvements in angina symptoms, myocardial perfusion reserve, or diastolic function. Only a subset of patients with severe CMD, defined by a CFR < 2.5, showed modest symptom improvement, suggesting ranolazine may still have a role in high-risk patients [ 88 ].

Outside of the USA, nicorandil (5 mg twice daily, with uptitration) has been commonly used as an alternative to long-acting nitrates over the past decades. Nicorandil exerts a dual mechanism of action as both a nitrate and an adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-sensitive potassium channel opener and has demonstrated a more pronounced effect on the coronary microvasculature compared with traditional nitrates [ 39 ]. Consequently, in patients with vasospastic angina, replacing long-acting nitrates with nicorandil may be an option. Nicorandil is unavailable in the USA owing to safety concerns, particularly its increased risk of gastrointestinal complications. One study showed a 43% higher risk of GI ulcers (25.8% incidence) and a 60% higher risk of GI perforations (1.6% incidence) over 3 years. In addition, it may cause skin, mucosal, and eye ulcerations, though these often resolve after discontinuation [ 39 , 89 ].

Practical Considerations in Angina Management The choice of initial therapy should consider patient-specific factors, including medication tolerance, comorbidities, hemodynamic profile, and local availability. Although a hierarchical approach utilizing first-line medications remains common, clinicians should recognize the flexibility in combining therapeutic agents. In addition, dosing frequency is a key consideration when prescribing medications, as regimens requiring multiple daily doses may reduce adherence and compromise therapeutic efficacy. Initial Therapy and Titration Beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers are appropriate first-line therapies for managing angina. For patients within 1 year of an MI, beta-blockers are the preferred choice. Beta-blocker therapy should aim to achieve a target resting heart rate of 55–60 bpm, provided the adjustment is well tolerated by the patient. Combining a beta-blocker with a calcium channel blocker, particularly a dihydropyridine agent, is an effective strategy for achieving optimal symptom control. However, rather than initiating dual therapy immediately, we advise initiation of monotherapy and waiting at least 2 weeks before adding a second agent if needed. This approach allows for careful dose titration to ensure tolerability. Furthermore, introducing medications sequentially facilitates the identification of the causative agent in the event of adverse effects.

If symptom control remains inadequate, additional agents such as ranolazine or nitrates should be considered. A large meta-analysis evaluating the relative efficacy of add-on antianginal therapies found that ranolazine provided the most consistent benefits across both exercise tolerance and clinical outcomes when added to a beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker [ 90 ]. Ivabradine can be considered in patients with HFrEF who need improved heart rate control. The choice of adjunctive therapy should align with the patient’s clinical profile; for example, ranolazine, given its mechanism of action, may be particularly beneficial in a patient with diabetes and CMD in need of an adjunctive antianginal medication with a neutral hemodynamic profile. Consideration of Angiographic Assessment and Revascularization PCI can be considered for patients with persistent angina despite optimized medical therapy, particularly those with significant quality-of-life impairment or a preference for more definitive symptom relief after understanding the risks and benefits. Angiographic assessment can aid in evaluating CMD or vasospasm to further refine therapy. The International Study of Comparative Health Effectiveness with Medical and Invasive Approaches (ISCHEMIA) trial demonstrated that patients with severe baseline angina experienced the greatest symptomatic relief from invasive strategies, but PCI did not reduce the risk of ischemic events or death over a median 3.2-year follow-up [ 91 ]. These findings underscore the importance of careful patient selection, emphasizing symptom burden and preferences when considering PCI alongside medical therapy.

Cardiac Rehabilitation While pharmacologic therapy plays an important role in managing angina, cardiac rehabilitation (CR) remains an integral component of comprehensive care for patients with cardiovascular disease. It carries a class I recommendation for those with stable angina, including those with ANOCA [ 8 ]. Among patients with MI treated with PCI, participation in a CR program has been shown to reduce angina recurrence and hospital readmissions. A meta-analysis by Yang et al. further supports that exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation is associated with significantly improved angina outcomes [ 92 ].

Despite proven benefits, CR remains underutilized, with only 24% of eligible patients participating and just 27% completing a full course [ 84 ]. Barriers include inadequate referral practices, socioeconomic disparities, limited access, and out-of-pocket costs. To address these challenges, mobile health-enabled CR (mHealth-CR) programs have emerged. These platforms deliver core components of traditional CR, such as exercise counseling and progress monitoring, remotely through smartphones and wearable devices. By enabling personalized, home-based rehabilitation, mHealth-CR offers a more accessible and personalized model of care.

While mHealth-CR has gained traction in general cardiac populations, its use in patients with CMD and ANOCA is understudied. The mHealth-Cardiac Rehabilitation for INOCA (INOCA-CARE) is an ongoing phase 2 trial evaluating a 3-month mobile health intervention amongst patients in this population [ 93 ].

Wearable devices used in mHealth-CR can monitor a patient’s heart rate and activity, allowing providers to individually tailor programs. This approach not only supports adherence but also expands access for patients facing logistical barriers [ 94 ]. Both home-based and center-based cardiac rehabilitation programs have been found to be equally effective in regard to clinical outcomes, exercise capacity, and quality of life [ 78 ]. Broader implementation of accessible, patient-centered CR approaches, particularly for those with CMD and ANOCA, represents an important opportunity to improve angina management and reduce disparities in care.

Adjunctive Cardioprotective Therapies Cardioprotective agents such as high-intensity statins and antihypertensives may also play an important role in the management of stable angina and CMD beyond atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk reduction. High-intensity statins are well known to slow atherosclerosis progression and reduce cardiovascular events. However, they may also serve a role on endothelial and microvascular function through pleiotropic effects. A 2023 meta-analysis of 20 randomized trials showed that high-intensity statin pretreatment significantly improved coronary microvascular function after PCI, as reflected by better thrombolysis in myocardial infarction (TIMI) flow and reduced index of microvascular resistance [ 95 ]. Similarly, renin–angiotensin system inhibitors are established in reducing cardiovascular events in patients with stable coronary disease [ 96 ]. However, they may also serve a purpose in patients with CMD, with one meta-analysis suggesting that angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors were associated with improvements in CFR among patients with CMD [ 97 ]. Data from studies such as the Women’s Ischemia Trial to Reduce Events in Non-obstructive CAD (WARRIOR) trial may further highlight benefits of combination therapy of statins and angiotensin-modifying agents [ 98 ].

Adjunctive Non-pharmacologic Interventions Enhanced external counterpulsation (EECP) is a noninvasive therapy for stable angina that uses sequential inflation and deflation of lower-extremity cuffs synchronized with the cardiac cycle to improve cardiac perfusion by increasing diastolic arterial pressure and retrograde aortic blood flow. MUST-EECP was a sham-controlled trial showing modest benefits for refractory stable angina, including a mean improvement of 37 s in time to ischemia and a statistically significant reduction in angina frequency among patients completing at least 34 sessions, with more active EECP patients achieving a 50% symptom improvement compared with the inactive group. However, no significant improvement in exercise capacity was observed. EECP can be considered for select patients with stable angina who are able to commit to 35 total hours of treatment over 4–7 weeks, though logistical challenges such as time commitment and limited availability hinder its broader use [ 99 ]. Use of EECP in patients with CMD is currently being investigated [ 100 ].

Transmyocardial laser revascularization (TMR) was explored as a last-resort treatment for patients with refractory angina. The procedure involves using a laser to create channels through the heart muscle and can be performed percutaneously or via thoracotomy. Although the mechanism of angina relief remains unclear, injury-induced angiogenesis has been proposed. However, TMR has fallen out of favor. A randomized controlled trial of the percutaneous approach with a placebo/sham control showed no clinical benefit and suggested a potential signal of harm [ 101 ]. Furthermore, when comparing TMR via thoracotomy with OMT, the risks of the procedure outweigh its potential benefits [ 102 ].

Investigational and Future Therapies Ongoing research using precision medicine holds promise for advancing CMD treatment. For example, Ford et al. identified a genetic risk locus associated with CMD and provided proof-of-concept data for zibotentan, an endothelin receptor antagonist, as a potential therapeutic option for this patient population [ 103 ]. The ENDORA-PCI trial is currently investigating the effects of the endothelin receptor antagonist ambrisentan in preventing microvascular dysfunction in patients with non-ST elevation ACS undergoing PCI, with the hope of extrapolating findings to those with microvascular angina [ 104 ]. In addition, ongoing research is exploring the potential role of eplerenone in the treatment of CMD [ 105 ].

For patients with ANOCA unresponsive to pharmacologic therapies, emerging options include the coronary sinus reducer, developed by Shockwave Medical (Santa Clara, California). Already available in Europe, it is currently under investigation in the USA. The coronary sinus reducer works by narrowing the coronary sinus, thereby increasing back pressure and enhancing perfusion to ischemic myocardium. A recent phase 2 trial evaluated its efficacy in patients with ANOCA confirmed through invasive angiographic testing. The study demonstrated that the device significantly improved angina symptoms, quality of life, and coronary microvascular function in patients with CMD [ 106 ]. Although this initial trial was not sham-controlled, the ongoing Coronary Sinus Reducer for Treatment of Refractory Angina (COSIRA)-2 trial, a multicenter, randomized (1:1 ratio), double-blinded, sham-controlled clinical trial, aims to further assess the efficacy of sinus reducers in this patient population [ 107 ].

In patients with refractory angina despite OMT and lacking further revascularization options, angiogenic gene therapy is under investigation. The Epicardial Delivery of XC001 Gene Therapy for Refractory Angina Coronary Treatment (EXACT) trial evaluated the safety and preliminary efficacy of XC001, a novel angiogenic gene therapy. In this phase 2 open-label trial, transepicardial administration of XC001 via surgical minithoracotomy significantly improved key clinical outcomes, including increased exercise duration (+ 115 s at 12 months), reduced ischemic burden on PET imaging, and decreased angina frequency (from 12.2 to 2.7 episodes/week over 12 months). While no adverse events were directly attributed to the therapy, the surgical delivery method carried procedural risks, highlighting the need for less invasive approaches. Catheter-based transendocardial delivery, which may offer a safer alternative, warrants further exploration. Additional research is needed to optimize delivery methods and assess long-term outcomes [ 108 ].

Autologous CD34 + cell therapy also represents a promising approach for patients with refractory angina who are not candidates for further revascularization. A meta-analysis of three randomized, double-blind trials demonstrated that intramyocardial administration of autologous CD34 + cells significantly improved total exercise time and reduced angina frequency. At 24 months, this therapy was associated with a notable reduction in all-cause mortality (12.1% versus 2.5%, P = 0.0025) and a trend toward fewer major adverse cardiovascular events [ 109 ]. These benefits are likely mediated through the pro-angiogenic properties of CD34 + endothelial progenitor cells. Although a pivotal phase 3 trial was initiated, it was prematurely discontinued for financial reasons. Nonetheless, this meta-analysis highlights the therapeutic potential of regenerative cell-based strategies for refractory angina. The ongoing CardiAMP Chronic Myocardial Ischemia trial is currently investigating transendocardial delivery of autologous bone marrow cells in this patient population [ 110 ].

Conclusions The management of chronic stable angina should include a patient-centered approach that prioritizes symptom relief, prevention of cardiac events, and enhancement of quality of life. OMT does not necessitate a rigid treatment hierarchy; rather, it should be tailored to individual patient needs, considering comorbidities, medication tolerance, and patient preferences to maximize adherence and therapeutic outcomes. Yet, OMT remains underutilized in real-world practice, with many patients undergoing diagnostic angiography or revascularization without first optimizing antianginal therapy.

While beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, and nitrates remain the cornerstone of angina management, additional agents such as ranolazine, ivabradine, and trimetazidine may be considered with refractory symptoms or contraindications to traditional therapies although geography, cost, and availability remain limitations. Additional research to better define their comparative effectiveness and ideal role in clinical practice is still needed. Notably, the past four decades have seen remarkably few novel therapeutic advancements for refractory angina, aside from ranolazine, ivabradine, and EECP. The development of new treatment modalities, including angiogenic gene therapy and interventional approaches such as the coronary sinus reducer and transendocardial stem cell delivery, represent a critical area for future investigation. In addition, further research and updated guidelines are warranted to refine the management of coronary microvascular dysfunction, an increasingly recognized contributor to angina.

Ultimately, optimizing medical management requires a careful balance of evidence-based strategies and personalized care to achieve the best possible clinical outcomes and quality of life for patients with chronic stable angina. The potential importance of both prevention and personal responsibility in controlling heart disease, the leading cause of death in the USA and elsewhere, has attracted renewed attention. Coronary artery disease is preventable, using relatively simple and inexpensive lifestyle changes. The inexorable rise in the prevalence of obesity, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and hypertension, often in the risk cluster known as the metabolic syndrome, drives the ever-increasing incidence of heart disease. Population-wide improvements in personal health habits appear to be a fundamental, evidence based public health measure, yet numerous barriers prevent implementation. A common symptom in patients with coronary artery disease, classical angina refers to the typical chest pressure or discomfort that results when myocardial oxygen demand rises and coronary blood flow is reduced by fixed, atherosclerotic, obstructive lesions. Different forms of angina and diagnosis, with a short description of the significance of pain and silent ischemia, are discussed in this review. The well accepted concept of myocardial oxygen imbalance in the genesis of angina is presented with new data about clinical pathology of stable angina and acute coronary syndromes. The roles of stress electrocardiography and stress myocardial perfusion scintigraphic imaging are reviewed, along with the information these tests provide about risk and prognosis. Finally, the current status of gender disparities in heart disease is summarized. Enhanced risk stratification and identification of patients in whom procedures will meaningfully change management is an ongoing quest. Current guidelines emphasize efficient triage of patients with suspected coronary artery disease. Many experts believe the predictive value of current decision protocols for coronary artery disease still needs improvement in order to optimize outcomes, yet avoid unnecessary coronary angiograms and radiation exposure. Coronary angiography remains the gold standard in the diagnosis of coronary artery obstructive disease.
